> Although most events given by participants were specific i.e. occurring at a particular time and place, some instances were not e.g. they extended over days or weeks.

> Following each event description participants completed a short self-report questionnaire that was constructed by the experimenters based upon previous measures of memory phenomenology (e.g.

> All participants were tested in-person and individually.

> Participants were asked to describe each event in as much detail as possible, refer to a specific place and time, and to choose an event lasting no longer than 24 hours.

> Before commencing the future condition, participants were instructed to imagine events that were both plausible and had not happened to them previously i.e. it needed to be novel.

> Once the participant had confirmed that their description was complete, they were asked to give their subjective ratings for the event.

> Therefore, we recruited 82 participants for Study 2.

> Participants completed three events for each valence (positive, negative) and temporal condition (past, future), with all events of one valence first and then the other (e.g. past positive, future positive, past negative, future negative).

> First, participants were presented with six positive and six negative cue words and explicitly instructed to describe events that were either positive or negative, respectively, in response to the cues.

> Second, participants had a time limit of one minute to describe each event (Cole et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2020).

> Since the participants had to describe some negative self-relevant events, they watched a short mood restoration video once all tasks were complete, of a ~1 minute clip from the TV show Friends (1994) (1995) (1996) (1997) (1998) (1999) (2000) (2001) (2002) (2003) (2004).

> Participants were explicitly told to generate a novel event which could plausibly happen to them in the future.

> Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study.

> In the main paper we detail the relationships that were found when participants were asked to rate the vividness and sense of (p)reliving, which are widely agreed core features of autonoetic experience for past and future events (Cordonnier et al., 2018; Habermas & Diel, 2013; Rubin et al., 2003 Rubin et al.,, 2019;; Zaman et al., 2024).

> Participants were also asked to give ratings for the clarity of their memories/imaginings broadly aligned to the internal detail subcategories of the AI.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To estimate statistical power, we used the Mixedpower R package (as suggested by Kumle et al., 2021), which facilitates simulation-based power analyses for LMMs. The simulations were based on the data from Study 1 using the final sample of n = 52. Because Mixedpower inherits the within-participant structure from the fitted model, these simulations reflected the Study 1 design of 10 autobiographical events per participant. The parameters for these simulations included the fixed effects of internal details and temporal condition, the number of participants was varied across 4 different plausible sample sizes (n = 62, 72, 82, 92), each sample size was subjected to 1000 simulations to ensure robust estimates, and the critical value for significance was set at 2 (Kumle et al., 2021). As Study 2 cued 12 events per participant, using the Study 1 structure with 10 events makes the resulting power estimates slightly conservative, as additional repeated measures increase precision without altering the fixed-effect estimates. The results of these simulations indicated that for both the vividness and (p)reliving models, n = 82 would achieve statistical power of 0.98 in predicting the relationship between number of internal details and subjective ratings (the fixed effect of internal details). Therefore, we recruited 82 participants for Study 2. These 82 healthy undergraduate students (67 female) were aged between 18-23 years (mean age = 19). There was no overlap in participants between studies.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.title: Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests
stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 4 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: Number of internal details was a significant predictor of vividness ratings (b = 0.030, SE = 0.006, F(1, 505) = 23.32, p < .001, for the full model: marginal R² = .15, conditional R² = .44) and (p)reliving ratings (b = 0.031, SE = 0.006, F(1, 515) = 31.72, p <.001, for the full model: marginal R² = .16, conditional R² = .47) 1 .
table.eta_coherence_note: Effect size reported but not verifiable from F and degrees of freedom alone.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Similarly, Wardell et al. (2021) assessed the correspondence between clarity/vividness judgements participants gave to memories with different emotional valences from recent and remote time periods and several episodic details from the AI.
In the AI all the details produced by the participant are categorised into an internal category, which describes the episodic content, or an external category, which contains non-episodic details.
Eightytwo healthy participants were recruited to take part in Study 1 in exchange for course credits.
For this experimenter, when participants gave little narrative or detail they did not consistently use standardised probes to elicit more information, whereas the other experimenters did.
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to testing.
Participants completed an adapted autobiographical cue word paradigm that probed both past and future events (Addis et al., 2008; Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974).
Participants were asked to generate events that were spatiotemporally specific and did not exceed 24 hours (Levine et al., 2002).
Although most events given by participants were specific i.e. occurring at a particular time and place, some instances were not e.g. they extended over days or weeks.
Following each event description participants completed a short self-report questionnaire that was constructed by the experimenters based upon previous measures of memory phenomenology (e.g.
All participants were tested in-person and individually.
Participants were asked to describe each event in as much detail as possible, refer to a specific place and time, and to choose an event lasting no longer than 24 hours.
Before commencing the future condition, participants were instructed to imagine events that were both plausible and had not happened to them previously i.e. it needed to be novel.
Once the participant had confirmed that their description was complete, they were asked to give their subjective ratings for the event.
Therefore, we recruited 82 participants for Study 2.

Participants completed three events for each valence (positive, negative) and temporal condition (past, future), with all events of one valence first and then the other (e.g. past positive, future positive, past negative, future negative).

First, participants were presented with six positive and six negative cue words and explicitly instructed to describe events that were either positive or negative, respectively, in response to the cues.
Second, participants had a time limit of one minute to describe each event (Cole et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2020).

Since the participants had to describe some negative self-relevant events, they watched a short mood restoration video once all tasks were complete, of a ~1 minute clip from the TV show Friends (1994) (1995) (1996) (1997) (1998) (1999) (2000) (2001) (2002) (2003) (2004).
Participants were explicitly told to generate a novel event which could plausibly happen to them in the future.
Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study.

In the main paper we detail the relationships that were found when participants were asked to rate the vividness and sense of (p)reliving, which are widely agreed core features of autonoetic experience for past and future events (Cordonnier et al., 2018; Habermas & Diel, 2013; Rubin et al., 2003 Rubin et al.,, 2019;; Zaman et al., 2024).
Participants were also asked to give ratings for the clarity of their memories/imaginings broadly aligned to the internal detail subcategories of the AI.

text.text: Memories for the personal past and imaginings of the future can be examined via the participant's subjective experience or a quantitative assessment of their episodic content.
There is ongoing debate as to the relationship between these measures.

Here we conducted two independent studies (n = 52 and 82) in healthy young adults who were presented with several cue words to prompt recollection of autobiographical memories and imaginings of possible future events.
They subsequently rated each of these experiences for its overall vividness and their sense of (p)reliving it.
The episodic content of each narrative was scored by the experimenter according to a standardised system (Autobiographical Interview; Levine et al., 2002).
text.formatted: The episodic content of each narrative was scored by the experimenter according to a standardised system (Autobiographical Interview; <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Levine et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Linear mixed-effects modelling, which can examine relationships on a trial-by-trial basis, revealed a significant association between subjective ratings and experimenterscored episodic content in both studies.

Further analysis revealed that within the episodic content category, the subcategories of event details (e.g. actions, people and objects, which are related to the narrative unfolding of events), and emotion/thought details were the primary ones significantly related to both the sense of vividness and (p)reliving.
Alignment tended to be stronger when imaging the future than recalling the past.
Our findings refute strong previous claims, based on suboptimal analyses, that quantitative measures of content and subjective ratings are distinct aspects of remembering.
Thus, episodic content meaningfully aligns with, but does not fully determine, subjective experiences of vividness and (p)reliving.
Further research is now required to determine the factors which might moderate this link.

A remarkable feature of the human mind is the ability to transport ourselves in time; to transcend the present moment, and either to mentally go back in time to remember our personal past or project ourselves into the future and imagine events that might happen (Atance & O'Neill, 2001; Brewer, 1992; Buckner & Carroll, 2007; Tulving, 1985; 2002).
text.formatted: A remarkable feature of the human mind is the ability to transport ourselves in time; to transcend the present moment, and either to mentally go back in time to remember our personal past or project ourselves into the future and imagine events that might happen <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Atance & O'Neill, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Brewer, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Buckner & Carroll, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Tulving, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">2002)</ref>.

text.text: This recollective/imaginative experience can evoke rich episodic content details, such as the people and objects present, spatiotemporal and sensory details, as well as remembering or eliciting emotions and thoughts (D'Argembeau & Van der Linden, 2006; Levine, 2004; Vannucci et al., 2020).

text.text: Early conceptualisations of episodic memory (Tulving, 1972) emphasised the importance of retrieved content, focusing on the personal event ("what"), the place that it happened ("where"), and the timing ("when").
text.formatted: Early conceptualisations of episodic memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Tulving, 1972)</ref> emphasised the importance of retrieved content, focusing on the personal event ("what"), the place that it happened ("where"), and the timing ("when").

text.text: However, Tulving's later writings stressed more the subjective aspects of remembering, introducing the notion of autonoetic consciousness, which is an awareness of oneself as a continuous entity through time (Tulving, 1985; 2002).
text.formatted: However, Tulving's later writings stressed more the subjective aspects of remembering, introducing the notion of autonoetic consciousness, which is an awareness of oneself as a continuous entity through time <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">(Tulving, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">2002)</ref>.

text.text: This awareness gives an individual the ability to engage in mental time travel, to both past events and imagined personal future events, and underpins the rich subjective (re-)experiencing of the event.
Tulving regarded autonoetic consciousness as a necessary and defining feature of episodic memory, which is not present in other forms of memory (Tulving, 1985; 2002; Wheeler et al., 1997).
text.formatted: Tulving regarded autonoetic consciousness as a necessary and defining feature of episodic memory, which is not present in other forms of memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">(Tulving, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">Wheeler et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: A fundamental issue in the literature is the link between the subjective experience of the individual, tapping autonoetic consciousness, and the behavioural retrieval of specific episodic event details in both episodic memory and future thinking.
There are a variety of ways of capturing participants' subjective experiences (see Folville et al., 2022; Sutin & Robins, 2007; Zaman et al., 2024).
text.formatted: There are a variety of ways of capturing participants' subjective experiences (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Folville et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">Sutin & Robins, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Zaman et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A longstanding measure used to tap autonoetic consciousness is the Remember/Know paradigm.

When participants indicate that they Remember previous events this is presumed to indicate an autonoetic episodic experience, whereas Know responses are noetic and are thought to be more linked to semantic memory information (Tulving, 1985 (Tulving, , 1989)).

text.text: However, there are several question marks over the extent to which the Remember/Know paradigm can capture, and separate, autonoetic and noetic awareness (see Rubin, 2005; Umanath & Coane, 2020; Zaman et al., 2024 for discussion).

text.text: An alternative way of examining autonoetic consciousness and the experience of mental time travel is to explicitly ask participants e.g. to what extent did you feel like you were (p)reliving the event?
(e.g. Cordonnier et al., 2018; Daselaar et al., 2008; Hassabis et al., 2007; Janssen et al., 2011; Rubin et al., 2003; 2019; Zaman et al., 2024).

text.text: There are other aspects of the subjective experience which participants can report upon that are argued to index autonoetic consciousness (Rubin & Umanath, 2015; Zaman et al., 2024).

text.text: The most prevalent measure is asking participants to report on the vividness of the experience (e.g. Armson et al., 2021; Baddeley & Andrade, 2000; Brewer & Pani, 1996; Giusberti et al., 1992; Johnson et al., 1988; Kensinger et al., 2011; Leer et al., 2014; Morton & MacLeod, 2023; Richter et al., 2016; Rubin, 2006; Rubin et al., 2003; Sheldon & Levine, 2013).

text.text: Memory vividness is generally thought to indicate the richness of the details in the event and clarity of the experience, as compared with the experience of actual perception (Brewer, 1992; D'Angiulli et al., 2013; Rubin et al., 2003).

text.text: Thus, autonoetic consciousness can be inferred by self-report ratings of memory qualities, including a sense of (p)reliving and contextually rich mental imagery (vividness).
An alternative way in which people's memories can be examined is via a quantitative assessment of specific episodic event details completed by the experimenter or another independent rater.
When examining episodic memory this is generally completed by scoring the accuracy of recollection.
For example, participants might be asked to retrieve contextual details from a previously presented study phase.
Autobiographical memories are more complex and tend to have more detailed and multifaceted representations compared to laboratory-based episodic memory tasks (Roediger & McDermott, 2013).
text.formatted: Autobiographical memories are more complex and tend to have more detailed and multifaceted representations compared to laboratory-based episodic memory tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Roediger & McDermott, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These can be scored by the experimenter for their accuracy (by corroborating with diaries or friends and family e.g. Barclay & Wellman, 1986) or narrative coherence (Reese at al., 2011), but most research examines the content of the memory, including how many episodic details it contains and perhaps of what type (e.g. Hassabis et al., 2007; Koriat et al., 2000; Schlagman et al., 2006; Vijayarajah et al., 2023).

text.text: As autobiographical memories contain episodic and non-episodic details e.g. semantic information (Brewer, 1992; Conway, 2001), the Autobiographical Interview protocol (AI; Levine et al., 2002) was developed to segregate these two memory types and to objectively quantify the amount and type of details that a participant recounts.
text.formatted: As autobiographical memories contain episodic and non-episodic details e.g. semantic information <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Brewer, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Conway, 2001)</ref>, the Autobiographical Interview protocol (AI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Levine et al., 2002)</ref> was developed to segregate these two memory types and to objectively quantify the amount and type of details that a participant recounts.

text.text: In the AI, the participant is asked to recall a past event in which they were personally involved, and which is specific to a certain time and place.
The details produced are then categorised by the experimenter as 'internal' or 'external'.
Internal details describe the episodic content, such as what happened, who was there, and the time and place of the event.
External details are non-episodic and comprise semantic details and information that is repeated or tangential to the main event described.
An extensive body of research has used this instrument to investigate autobiographical memory (see: https://levinelab.weebly.com/ai-bibliography.html)).
text.formatted: An extensive body of research has used this instrument to investigate autobiographical memory (see: <ref type="url" target="https://levinelab.weebly.com/ai-bibliography.html)">https://levinelab.weebly.com/ai-bibliography.html</ref>).

text.text: More recently it has been adapted to examine episodic future thinking (e.g. Addis et al., 2008; Reed & Evans, 2024; Williams et al., 2020).
text.formatted: More recently it has been adapted to examine episodic future thinking (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Addis et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Reed & Evans, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Williams et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This is consistent with Tulving's notion of mental time travel being bidirectional (Tulving, 1985 (Tulving, , 2002) ) and the constructive episodic simulation hypothesis (Schacter & Addis, 2007), which proposes that episodic memory supports the construction of imagined future events by the retrieval and flexible recombination of stored information into a new scenario.

text.text: According to Levine (2004, page 56) the AI (Levine et al., 2002) "transfers this burden of self-report from the participant to the experimenter" and "assumes that details reflecting specific happenings, perceptual information, or mental states reflect episodic recollection (operationalized as ''internal'' details)".

text.text: It might therefore be anticipated that participants' phenomenological reports of autobiographical memory and the behavioural retrieval of specific episodic event details would be well correlated dimensions of remembering.
This might be particularly so as AI internal (episodic) details are scored using categories adapted from a subjective measure of memory: the Memory Characteristics Questionnaire.

This was originally developed by Johnson et al. (1988) to distinguish memories of experienced events, which contain more sensory and contextual details, from memories of imagined events, which contain more elements related to cognitive operations.

text.text: Some studies have examined the correlation between experimenter scored internal details on the AI and trait questionnaires (e.g.

The Survey of Autobiographical Memory, Palombo et al., 2013; The Autobiographical Recollection Test, Berntsen et al., 2019) completed by participants assessing their past memory or future episodic thinking.
text.formatted: The Survey of Autobiographical Memory, <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Palombo et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">The Autobiographical Recollection Test, Berntsen et al., 2019)</ref> completed by participants assessing their past memory or future episodic thinking.

text.text: These findings paint a mixed picture.

While there is some evidence for associations between these measures (e.g. Armson et al., 2021; Matsumoto et al., 2022; Palombo et al., 2013; Setton et al., 2021), there are also numerous instances where significant relationships have not been found (e.g. Clark & Maguire, 2020; Matsumoto et al., 2022; Palombo et al., 2013; Setton et al., 2021).
text.formatted: While there is some evidence for associations between these measures (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Armson et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Matsumoto et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Palombo et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Setton et al., 2021)</ref>, there are also numerous instances where significant relationships have not been found (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Clark & Maguire, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Matsumoto et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Palombo et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Setton et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, there is a mismatch.

The AI is an event-based instrument wherein the participant recounts a specific experience, whereas the questionnaires tap trait mnemonics, i.e. general tendencies in how individuals recall memories (Palombo et al., 2018; see Aytürk et al., 2024, for the more general point that trait and event level phenomenology do not correlate strongly in autobiographical memory).
text.formatted: The AI is an event-based instrument wherein the participant recounts a specific experience, whereas the questionnaires tap trait mnemonics, i.e. general tendencies in how individuals recall memories <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Palombo et al., 2018</ref>; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Aytürk et al., 2024</ref>, for the more general point that trait and event level phenomenology do not correlate strongly in autobiographical memory).

text.text: Other studies have looked at both subjective and quantitative episodic measures at the event level by asking participants for their phenomenological ratings after each narration.

Even using this approach Clark and Maguire (2020) did not find a significant relationship between subjective vividness and episodic (internal) detail of memories using the AI in over 200 healthy volunteers.
text.formatted: Even using this approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Clark and Maguire (2020)</ref> did not find a significant relationship between subjective vividness and episodic (internal) detail of memories using the AI in over 200 healthy volunteers.

text.text: Based on this null result they concluded that internal details on the AI might not reflect the participant's subjective experiences of remembering and they may in fact "be measuring different things" (page 21).

Similarly, Wardell et al. (2021) assessed the correspondence between clarity/vividness judgements participants gave to memories with different emotional valences from recent and remote time periods and several episodic details from the AI.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">Wardell et al. (2021)</ref> assessed the correspondence between clarity/vividness judgements participants gave to memories with different emotional valences from recent and remote time periods and several episodic details from the AI.

text.text: No significant relationships were observed after correcting for multiple comparisons.
However, Lockrow et al. (2024) in a sample of healthy younger and older adults did find a significant, albeit small, association between episodic detail and vividness.
text.formatted: However, <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Lockrow et al. (2024)</ref> in a sample of healthy younger and older adults did find a significant, albeit small, association between episodic detail and vividness.

text.text: Thus, empirical work largely does not support there being a link between vividness, which is thought to index autonoetic consciousness, and episodic recollection on the AI when examining autobiographical memory.
There are very few studies that have examined this link in episodic future thinking.

This is surprising as while there are many commonalities in their cognitive processes, phenomenology, and neural basis (e.g. Addis et al., 2007; Cordonnier et al., 2018; Schacter et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2007); there are also differences (Suddendorf, 2010).

text.text: For example, autobiographical memories are typically richer in sensory details, more vivid and spatially coherent than imagined future events (De Brigard & Giovanello, 2012; Rubin, 2014).

text.text: Future events often display a positivity bias (adults imagine better futures), which is not typically present in memories of past events (Rasmussen & Berntsen, 2013).

text.text: These differences in phenomenology mean that it is unclear whether associations will also be present for episodic future thinking, and if so, whether they would be equivalent in magnitude.

This was examined by Thakral et al. (2020) who placed young healthy volunteers in an MRI scanner, where they were asked to imagine personal future events in response to cues and then to assess the vividness of the construction on each trial.

text.text: Outside the scanner participants reported what they had thought about in the scanner and these narratives were scored using the AI.
On an individual participant basis, correlations were computed between vividness ratings and internal details on the AI for that event.

Across participants it was found that these correlations were significantly greater than zero, but small in magnitude (although note that the authors conclude that vividness ratings and internal details "operate via distinct neural mechanisms"; Thakral et al., 2020, page 10).

text.text: Recently, Zaman et al. (2024) completed an exploratory factor analysis of subjective ratings given by healthy young adults in an autobiographical memory and future thinking task and identified a 'core autonoetic consciousness' factor for each temporal direction, on which vividness and (p)re-experiencing ratings loaded highly.
text.formatted: Recently, <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Zaman et al. (2024)</ref> completed an exploratory factor analysis of subjective ratings given by healthy young adults in an autobiographical memory and future thinking task and identified a 'core autonoetic consciousness' factor for each temporal direction, on which vividness and (p)re-experiencing ratings loaded highly.

text.text: However, there were no significant relationships between this factor and participants' episodic detail scores from the AI for either past or future events.

In summary, there has been limited work examining the relationship between participants' subjective ratings and episodic content details in future thinking and the results from this work portray an unclear picture.
It is possible that this relationship has been occluded or attenuated by the way in which researchers typically examine it.
It is usual for participants to recount several autobiographical or imagined future experiences and to give phenomenological ratings after each of them.

The scores for each type of memory measure are totalled/averaged across trials, and these summary statistics are correlated across all participants i.e. this examines the relationship between the average rating on the subjective measure and the average rating on the quantitative content measure.
Therefore, this approach does not allow for a direct comparison between participants' memory ratings and the amount of episodic content of specific memories/imagined events.
It ignores the nested structure of the memories and the impact of both individual differences and the cues themselves (Aytürk et al., 2024), which reduces statistical power (Wright, 1998).

text.text: Alternative approaches, such as linear mixed-effects modelling (LMM; Baayen et al., 2008) can assess this relationship on a trial-wise basis and are appropriate for the clustered structure of the data, due to each participant contributing multiple experiences.

text.text: This approach has been used, for example, to determine the correspondence between memory accuracy and memory confidence (Wong et al., 2012) and the relationship between internal and external scores on the AI (Devitt et al., 2017).

text.text: In the latter study when the authors reanalysed data using LMM, they found several significant negative relationships between AI internal and external details that were not evident when using averaged correlations, highlighting that this approach can be more sensitive.
Our aim in the current work was to provide a more comprehensive assessment of the relation between subjective ratings, tapping autonoetic consciousness, and quantitative measures of episodic content.

The internal dimension of the AI (Levine et al., 2002) was designed to capture episodic retrieval i.e. autonoetic consciousness and the experience of mental time travel, so it is important for validation to assess this link.

text.text: Previous studies have made strong claims based on finding no link between quantitative measures of episodic content and participants' report of the phenomenological qualities of the event.

For example, Clark and Maguire (2020; page 21) stated that "AI internal details…might not reflect an individual's subjective experience of memory recall" and Zaman et al. (2024, page 14) concluded that "experimenter derived memory scores may tap into separate aspects of remembering than the selfreport questions used to characterize subjective experience".
However, these conclusions are based upon studies which aggregated memories or only used a single memory, respectively.
A more appropriate method to address this question is LMM, as it takes into consideration person and memory level effects (Wright, 1998).

text.text: We conducted two independent studies in which healthy young adults were presented with cue words and asked to recollect a personal episode from the past or to imagine a plausible personal event in the future involving that word.

Study 1 used cue words that were predominantly positive (without any explicit instructions regarding valence), whereas Study 2 employed cue words and instructions designed to prompt both positively and negatively valenced events.

Two key phenomenological ratings were gathered from participants after each narrative: vividness and the sense of (p)reliving, both of which appear to be integral to autonoetic consciousness (Rubin, 2005; Rubin & Umanath, 2015; Zaman et al., 2024).

text.text: Participants' narratives were scored according to the established AI protocol (Levine et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Participants' narratives were scored according to the established AI protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Levine et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In the AI all the details produced by the participant are categorised into an internal category, which describes the episodic content, or an external category, which contains non-episodic details.
The internal score is comprised of several subcategories.
Event describes what happened (i.e. the narrative core of the episode) and includes objects and who was there.
Time indicates temporal details, while place includes any information involving scene layout and localisation in space.
Perceptual details are those from any sensory modality, and the emotion/thought category describes details related to the mental state of the participant at the time of the event.
See Table 1 for more details on AI scoring.
text.formatted: See Table <ref type="table">1</ref> for more details on AI scoring.

text.text: We predicted that there would be significant associations between participants' phenomenological ratings (vividness and sense of (p)reliving) and episodic content, as indexed by AI internal details, using a more sensitive analysis (LMM), which can examine this relationship at the trial level.

Moreover, we also wanted to examine this in a more nuanced way by examining the subcategories of the AI, which might help us to understand what type of episodic details may be driving subjective ratings of vividness and (p)reliving.

While perceptual detail (Cooper & Ritchey, 2022; Dawes et al., 2022; Rubin, 2005; St-Laurent et al., 2009 , 2015), emotion (Kensinger et al., 2011; Phelps & Sharot, 2008; St Jacques & Levine, 2007; Talarico et al., 2004) and narrative quality (Habermas & Diel, 2013; Nelson et al. 2008 Nelson et al. , 2021) ) may all contribute, prominent recent accounts (Hassabis & Maguire, 2007; Robin, 2018; Rubin & Umanath, 2015; see also Gaffan, 1991) consider autobiographical memories, and their defining subjective properties, as fundamentally dependent on mental scene construction.

text.text: Thus, a further aim was to determine which episodic detail type(s) might demonstrate greater correspondence to people's subjective experiences.
All associations will be examined for past memory and future imagining to determine if they hold across both temporal directions and are of similar magnitude.
Our findings provide important new evidence to inform the debate around the relationship between episodic memory content and recollective experience.
>Study 1 -Method
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Study 1 -Method</head>

text.text: As this study was exploratory, no a priori power calculation was performed (Ditroilo et al., 2025).
text.formatted: As this study was exploratory, no a priori power calculation was performed <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Ditroilo et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Eightytwo healthy participants were recruited to take part in Study 1 in exchange for course credits.
Of these 82 participants, 30 were excluded due to a systematic error wherein one experimenter did not follow the standard AI procedure.
The transcripts for participants interviewed by this experimenter had markedly lower word counts.
The mean word count for this experimenter was 816 words (based on 30 transcripts) versus 1552 words (Experimenter 2, based on 30 transcripts) and 1387 words (Experimenter 3, based on 22 transcripts).
For this experimenter, when participants gave little narrative or detail they did not consistently use standardised probes to elicit more information, whereas the other experimenters did.
Thus, a decision was taken during AI scoring, prior to analysis, to omit all data collected by this experimenter.
The remaining sample comprised 52 undergraduate students (46 female) who were aged between 18-39 years (mean age = 20) and were fluent in English.
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to testing.
This research was reviewed and approved by Cardiff University School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee (EC.07.03.06.1209GA11).
>Materials
text.formatted: <head n="2.2." >Materials</head>

text.text: Participants completed an adapted autobiographical cue word paradigm that probed both past and future events (Addis et al., 2008; Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974).
text.formatted: Participants completed an adapted autobiographical cue word paradigm that probed both past and future events <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Addis et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974)</ref>.

text.text: A series of ten cue words (Holiday, University, Home, Day Trip, Party, Family, Pets/Animals, Christmas, Shopping, Birthday) were selected by the experimenters.

For those words which could be found in The Glasgow Norms (Scott et al., 2019) the mean valence rating was 7.25 (6.21-7.91) on a scale ranging from 1 (very negative) to 9 (very positive), arousal was 6.08 (4.84-7.52) on a scale ranging from 1 (very low arousal) to 9 (very high arousal), and imageability was 5.87 (4.97-6.65) on a scale ranging from 1 (very unimageable) to 7 (very imageable).
text.formatted: For those words which could be found in The Glasgow Norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Scott et al., 2019)</ref> the mean valence rating was 7.25 (6.21-7.91) on a scale ranging from 1 (very negative) to 9 (very positive), arousal was 6.08 (4.84-7.52) on a scale ranging from 1 (very low arousal) to 9 (very high arousal), and imageability was 5.87 (4.97-6.65) on a scale ranging from 1 (very unimageable) to 7 (very imageable).

text.text: Cue words were presented both orally and visually (using cue cards) to solicit production of both past and future events, with half in each temporal direction (past, future).
Participants were asked to generate events that were spatiotemporally specific and did not exceed 24 hours (Levine et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Participants were asked to generate events that were spatiotemporally specific and did not exceed 24 hours <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Levine et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, future events were required to be novel and plausible given the participant's current plans (Addis et al., 2008).
text.formatted: In addition, future events were required to be novel and plausible given the participant's current plans <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Addis et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Participants described five events for one temporal direction (past or future) before beginning the next condition, with the order counterbalanced across participants.
The allocation of cue words to condition was also counterbalanced, with a fixed order in each condition.
Participant responses were audio recorded by the experimenter.
The audio recordings were transcribed and scored according to the standardised AI scoring protocol (Levine et al., 2002).
text.formatted: The audio recordings were transcribed and scored according to the standardised AI scoring protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Levine et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Psychometric evaluation of the AI scoring has demonstrated high inter-rater reliability, replicable age effects, robust internal consistency across timepoints, and positive correlations with standard, performance-based episodic memory tasks (Lockrow et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Psychometric evaluation of the AI scoring has demonstrated high inter-rater reliability, replicable age effects, robust internal consistency across timepoints, and positive correlations with standard, performance-based episodic memory tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Lockrow et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: First, responses were segmented into distinct sections to score for internal and external details.
Details were typically grammatical clauses referencing a unique occurrence, observation or thought (Levine et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Details were typically grammatical clauses referencing a unique occurrence, observation or thought <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Levine et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Details were then scored as internal if they directly pertained to the main event and external if they were unrelated to the main event (Levine et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Details were then scored as internal if they directly pertained to the main event and external if they were unrelated to the main event <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Levine et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Although most events given by participants were specific i.e. occurring at a particular time and place, some instances were not e.g. they extended over days or weeks.
These were not excluded.

For these cases, as outlined in the AI scoring manual, the scorer needed to define the main event (the one described in the most detail) and then categorise segments that were part of this event (internal details) separately from those that were not (external details).
Internal responses were subcategorised into event, time, place, perceptual, and emotion/thought details, see Table 1.
text.formatted: Internal responses were subcategorised into event, time, place, perceptual, and emotion/thought details, see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: In a slight adjustment to the original AI scoring, one's own orientation in space e.g.
"I was to the right of Carl" was coded under place, rather than as a perceptual detail (see Hodgetts et al., 2017 and Williams et al., 2020, who also coded this way).
text.formatted: "I was to the right of Carl" was coded under place, rather than as a perceptual detail (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Hodgetts et al., 2017 and</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Williams et al., 2020</ref>, who also coded this way).

text.text: Scoring was completed by two independent raters trained on the coding scheme.
The two raters blind double-scored the first 8 participant's transcripts i.e. 80 memories/future events (10% of the original sample e.g. see Cole et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The two raters blind double-scored the first 8 participant's transcripts i.e. 80 memories/future events (10% of the original sample e.g. see <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Cole et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: An intra-class correlation analysis (ICC; two-way random model) was conducted in IBM SPSS Statistics (Version 26) on these data to evaluate the inter-rater consistency across all AI subcategories.

Significant ICCs (all ps < .01) were observed for both the broader categories (internal: r = 0.99; external: r = 0.97) and their subcategories (internal: event r = 0.99; time r = 0.99; place r = 0.99; perceptual r = 0.93; emotion/thought r = 0.94).
text.formatted: Significant ICCs (all ps < .01) were observed for both the broader categories (internal: r = 0.99; external: r = 0.97) and their subcategories (internal: event r = 0.99; time r = 0.99; place r = 0.99; perceptual r = 0.93; emotion/thought r = 0.94).

text.text: For subsequent transcripts these were scored by one rater and checked by the other to maintain scoring fidelity.
Any discrepancies were resolved by discussion between the raters.
Experimenters were blind to the hypotheses of the study.

Following each event description participants completed a short self-report questionnaire that was constructed by the experimenters based upon previous measures of memory phenomenology (e.g.
Autobiographical Memory Questionnaire, Rubin et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Autobiographical Memory Questionnaire, <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Rubin et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: All questions were rated on a 7-point Likert scale.

Individual items assessed the overall vividness of each event ('The overall vividness of this event was…';1 = not vivid,7 = very vivid) and the participant's sense of (p)reliving ('To what extent did you feel you were experiencing this memory/future scenario as if you were actually there?' ;1 = not at all,7 = It felt like I was really there).
Correlations were modest between vividness and (p)reliving ratings (past: τb = 0.47, future: τb = 0.58, both ps < .001), indicating that these ratings are not redundant.
text.formatted: Correlations were modest between vividness and (p)reliving ratings (past: τb = 0.47, future: τb = 0.58, both ps < .001), indicating that these ratings are not redundant.

text.text: Previous research has suggested that overall vividness and feelings of (p)reliving are core features of autonoetic experience for past and future events (Cordonnier et al., 2018; Habermas & Diel, 2013; Rubin et al., 2003 Rubin et al., , 2019;; Zaman et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Previous research has suggested that overall vividness and feelings of (p)reliving are core features of autonoetic experience for past and future events <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Cordonnier et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Habermas & Diel, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Rubin et al., 2003</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Rubin et al., , 2019;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Zaman et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Ratings were also given (1 = not at all clear,7 = extremely clear and distinct) for the clarity of episodic details for the following attributes: event/perceptual ('Details including people, objects, and surroundings are...'), time ('The time in which this event takes place is...'), place ('The location where this event takes place is...') and emotions/thoughts ('My own thoughts and feelings when the event takes place are...').
These additional ratings are not examined in the main text but see the Supplementary Results for complementary analyses of the relationship between these ratings and the AI subcategories.
All participants were tested in-person and individually.

The experimenter explained that participants would be presented with a series of cue words and that they were to use each word to either remember an event from the past or imagine an event involving themselves in the future.
It was clarified whether the past or future condition would take place first and that they would be notified before commencing the next condition.
Participants were asked to describe each event in as much detail as possible, refer to a specific place and time, and to choose an event lasting no longer than 24 hours.
Before commencing the future condition, participants were instructed to imagine events that were both plausible and had not happened to them previously i.e. it needed to be novel.
There were no constraints on the recency of events that were described i.e. participants could describe past and future events within any time frame.

In the instance that a participant failed to provide sufficient detail or generated an event that was not very specific, they were probed using a standardised prompt such as 'Are there any other specific details you can think of?'.
The experimenter presented each cue word on a cue card, as well as stating it orally as part of the standardised instructions.
No limit was implemented on the amount of time participants took to describe each event.
Once the participant had confirmed that their description was complete, they were asked to give their subjective ratings for the event.
This procedure was repeated for all ten cue words.
Linear mixed-effects modelling (LMM) was used to assess the relationship between internal details and participant ratings (vividness and (p)reliving) on a trial-by-trial basis.
Linear mixed-effects modelling using the GAMLj package (Gallucci, 2023) was implemented in Jamovi (Version 2.4.8; The jamovi project, 2023).
text.formatted: Linear mixed-effects modelling using the GAMLj package <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Gallucci, 2023)</ref> was implemented in Jamovi (Version 2.4.8; The jamovi project, 2023).

text.text: The models treated the participants and cue words as random effects (Wright, 1998).
text.formatted: The models treated the participants and cue words as random effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">(Wright, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: More specifically, the models included random intercepts for both participant and cue words.
In all models, the dependent variable was the participant ratings, number of internal details was a continuous predictor, and the temporal condition (past or future) was a categorical predictor.
The interaction between internal details and temporal condition was also examined to determine if these relationships differed by temporal condition.
Internal details and temporal condition were added as fixed effects.

It should be noted that GAMLj: i) automatically mean-centres all continuous predictors to ensure that the range of any newly created variables (i.e. interactions) are kept around the means of the data, which helps with interpretation of the data and improves the chances of convergence (Enders & Tofighi, 2007) and ii) implements the Satterthwaite method for degrees of freedom, which leads to differences in the denominator degrees of freedom between different analyses.
text.formatted: It should be noted that GAMLj: i) automatically mean-centres all continuous predictors to ensure that the range of any newly created variables (i.e. interactions) are kept around the means of the data, which helps with interpretation of the data and improves the chances of convergence <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Enders & Tofighi, 2007)</ref> and ii) implements the Satterthwaite method for degrees of freedom, which leads to differences in the denominator degrees of freedom between different analyses.

text.text: The contrast coding of the categorical predictor was set to 'simple' which means the first group was compared to the subsequent groups whilst centring the contrast to 0.

As the first and subsequent groups are defined by alphanumeric order, the future condition was the first group, and the past condition was the subsequent group (futurepast); the mean of the future condition was compared against the mean of the past condition.

Two of these models were examined between: i) experimenter scored number of internal details and participant rated vividness of each event and ii) experimenter scored number of internal details and participant rated sense of (p)reliving of each event.

General linear models (GLM) were used to investigate the extent to which the number of details of each of the AI subcategories (event, perceptual, time, place and emotion/thought details) predicted participant ratings (vividness and (p)reliving) on a trial-by-trial basis.
Alike the linear mixed-effects models, GLM were implemented in Jamovi (Version 2.4.8; The jamovi project, 2023) using GAMLj (Gallucci, 2023).
text.formatted: Alike the linear mixed-effects models, GLM were implemented in Jamovi (Version 2.4.8; The jamovi project, 2023) using GAMLj <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Gallucci, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In both the GLMs, the dependent variable was the participant ratings, the number of details from each of the AI subcategories were continuous predictors, and the temporal condition (past or future) was a categorical predictor.
The interaction between each AI subcategory and temporal condition was also examined to determine if these relationships differed by temporal condition.
Therefore, the GLMs were used to perform a moderated regression on a trial-by-trial basis (Lorah, 2022).
text.formatted: Therefore, the GLMs were used to perform a moderated regression on a trial-by-trial basis <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Lorah, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Two of these models were implemented, wherein the dependent variable was either i) vividness or ii) (p)reliving ratings.

text.text: ICCs were examined for internal details, overall vividness ratings, and (p)reliving ratings for each temporal condition.
These all indicated poor consistency across trials (all rs < 0.51, full results are reported in the Supplementary Results), providing further justification for our trial-level LMM analyses.

Summary of Study 1 findings and rationale for Study 2

Linear mixed-effects modelling (LMM; Wright, 1998) demonstrated that there was a significant and positive relationship between the number of episodic details as scored by the AI protocol (Levine et al., 2002) and both ratings of vividness and (p)reliving provided by the participant.
text.formatted: Linear mixed-effects modelling (LMM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Wright, 1998)</ref> demonstrated that there was a significant and positive relationship between the number of episodic details as scored by the AI protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Levine et al., 2002)</ref> and both ratings of vividness and (p)reliving provided by the participant.

text.text: This was found for both autobiographical past and future events.

In contrast, correlations conducted on quantitative episodic content and subjective phenomenological ratings that were summed across events revealed significant relationships in the episodic future thinking condition only.

Furthermore, GLM demonstrated that, within the internal category, thought to reflect episodic autobiographical content (Levine et al., 2002), event and emotion/thought details were significant predictors of overall vividness and (p)reliving ratings for past and future events.
text.formatted: Furthermore, GLM demonstrated that, within the internal category, thought to reflect episodic autobiographical content <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Levine et al., 2002)</ref>, event and emotion/thought details were significant predictors of overall vividness and (p)reliving ratings for past and future events.

text.text: Given that these findings contradict claims made in previous work (e.g. Clark & Maguire, 2020; Zaman et al., 2024), a second study was run with a larger sample to determine if these results would replicate.
text.formatted: Given that these findings contradict claims made in previous work (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Clark & Maguire, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Zaman et al., 2024)</ref>, a second study was run with a larger sample to determine if these results would replicate.

text.text: As prior work indicates that the majority of variance in self-reported phenomenology (including vividness and reliving) is attributable not to individual differences in autobiographical memory ability, but to individual memories and their cues (Aytürk et al., 2024), in Study 2 we manipulated cue characteristics.
text.formatted: As prior work indicates that the majority of variance in self-reported phenomenology (including vividness and reliving) is attributable not to individual differences in autobiographical memory ability, but to individual memories and their cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Aytürk et al., 2024)</ref>, in Study 2 we manipulated cue characteristics.

text.text: As previous research has indicated that positive and negative events differ in the amount of episodic detail in which they are described (Ford et al., 2012; Holland & Kensinger, 2010; St Jacques & Levine, 2007) as well as how they are rated by participants (D' Argembeau & van der Linden, 2004; Kensinger & Schacter, 2006; Rasmussen & Berntsen, 2013; Simpson & Sheldon, 2020), cue word valence may be an important cue-level factor that moderates the relationship between quantitative episodic content measures and subjective experience.
text.formatted: As previous research has indicated that positive and negative events differ in the amount of episodic detail in which they are described <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Ford et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Holland & Kensinger, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">St Jacques & Levine, 2007)</ref> as well as how they are rated by participants (D' <ref type="bibr">Argembeau & van der Linden, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Kensinger & Schacter, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Rasmussen & Berntsen, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Simpson & Sheldon, 2020)</ref>, cue word valence may be an important cue-level factor that moderates the relationship between quantitative episodic content measures and subjective experience.

text.text: Whereas Study 1 employed predominantly positively valenced cue words, Study 2 included both positive and negative cue words.
Thus, Study 2 allowed us to determine the replicability of results from Study 1 as well as whether they would generalise when negatively valenced cue words were used.
All methodological details for Study 2 are the same as for Study 1 except as indicted below.
To estimate statistical power, we used the Mixedpower R package (as suggested by Kumle et al., 2021), which facilitates simulation-based power analyses for LMMs.
text.formatted: To estimate statistical power, we used the Mixedpower R package (as suggested by <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Kumle et al., 2021)</ref>, which facilitates simulation-based power analyses for LMMs.

text.text: The simulations were based on the data from Study 1 using the final sample of n = 52.
Because Mixedpower inherits the within-participant structure from the fitted model, these simulations reflected the Study 1 design of 10 autobiographical events per participant.

The parameters for these simulations included the fixed effects of internal details and temporal condition, the number of participants was varied across 4 different plausible sample sizes (n = 62, 72, 82, 92), each sample size was subjected to 1000 simulations to ensure robust estimates, and the critical value for significance was set at 2 (Kumle et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The parameters for these simulations included the fixed effects of internal details and temporal condition, the number of participants was varied across 4 different plausible sample sizes (n = 62, 72, 82, 92), each sample size was subjected to 1000 simulations to ensure robust estimates, and the critical value for significance was set at 2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Kumle et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: As Study 2 cued 12 events per participant, using the Study 1 structure with 10 events makes the resulting power estimates slightly conservative, as additional repeated measures increase precision without altering the fixed-effect estimates.

The results of these simulations indicated that for both the vividness and (p)reliving models, n = 82 would achieve statistical power of 0.98 in predicting the relationship between number of internal details and subjective ratings (the fixed effect of internal details).
Therefore, we recruited 82 participants for Study 2.
These 82 healthy undergraduate students (67 female) were aged between 18-23 years (mean age = 19).
There was no overlap in participants between studies.
In the second study, the AI scoring system (Levine et al., 2002) and participant ratings were consistent with the first study.
text.formatted: In the second study, the AI scoring system <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Levine et al., 2002)</ref> and participant ratings were consistent with the first study.

text.text: However, the cue word paradigm for past/future events (Addis et al., 2008; Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974) was adapted to include both normatively positive (Birthday, Achievement, Adventurous, School/University, Christmas, Holiday) and negative (Exam, Falling Over, Getting into Trouble, Failing, Embarrassed, Mistake) cue words that were selected by the experimenters.
text.formatted: However, the cue word paradigm for past/future events <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Addis et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974)</ref> was adapted to include both normatively positive (Birthday, Achievement, Adventurous, School/University, Christmas, Holiday) and negative (Exam, Falling Over, Getting into Trouble, Failing, Embarrassed, Mistake) cue words that were selected by the experimenters.

text.text: All participants for Study 2 were also tested in-person and individually, but two adaptations were made to the procedure.

First, participants were presented with six positive and six negative cue words and explicitly instructed to describe events that were either positive or negative, respectively, in response to the cues.
Second, participants had a time limit of one minute to describe each event (Cole et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2020).

text.text: One minute was selected to maximise efficiency and to reduce the cognitive burden on participants.
