text.text: According to Tulving (2002), episodic autobiographical memory is the conscious recollection of a specific event from one's personal past.
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Tulving (2002)</ref>, episodic autobiographical memory is the conscious recollection of a specific event from one's personal past.

text.text: Episodic memory has also been proposed to form part of a broader capacity for mental time travel, enabling conscious awareness of past experiences and the imagination of specific future events (Tulving, 2005).
text.formatted: Episodic memory has also been proposed to form part of a broader capacity for mental time travel, enabling conscious awareness of past experiences and the imagination of specific future events <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">(Tulving, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: This capacity, often described as autonoetic consciousness, is typically assessed through self-report measures of phenomenological qualities such as vividness and a sense of (p)reliving (Habermas & Diel, 2013; Rubin et al., 2003 Rubin et al., , 2019;; Zaman et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This capacity, often described as autonoetic consciousness, is typically assessed through self-report measures of phenomenological qualities such as vividness and a sense of (p)reliving <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Habermas & Diel, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Rubin et al., 2003</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Rubin et al., , 2019;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Zaman et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Subjective memory experience and the retrieval of episodic details might be expected to correlate, particularly because the Autobiographical Interview (AI) coding protocol was developed from a phenomenological framework (Johnson et al., 1988; Levine et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Subjective memory experience and the retrieval of episodic details might be expected to correlate, particularly because the Autobiographical Interview (AI) coding protocol was developed from a phenomenological framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Johnson et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Levine et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence for such an association has been inconsistent, leading some researchers to argue that subjective experience and episodic content reflect distinct aspects of remembering (e.g. Clark & Maguire, 2020; Zaman et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, evidence for such an association has been inconsistent, leading some researchers to argue that subjective experience and episodic content reflect distinct aspects of remembering (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Clark & Maguire, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Zaman et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A limitation of much of this work is that it has overlooked the multilevel structure of autobiographical events, treating memories as independent observations or aggregating across events (Aytürk et al., 2024; Wright, 1998).
text.formatted: A limitation of much of this work is that it has overlooked the multilevel structure of autobiographical events, treating memories as independent observations or aggregating across events <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Aytürk et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Wright, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: To address this issue, we used multilevel modelling to examine trial-by-trial associations between subjective phenomenology and episodic content across both temporal directions.
Across two independent studies, a significant link was found between subjective recollective experience and the quantity of episodic content, supporting our hypothesis.

More specifically, we found that the number of episodic details, based on the AI coding scheme, was significantly associated with the ratings provided by the participant for both vividness and sense of (p)reliving across both autobiographical past and future events.
Furthermore, analyses of individual AI subcategories indicated that event and emotion/thought details were most consistently associated with phenomenological ratings.
These findings suggest that subjective autonoetic experience and quantitative measures of episodic content are related, despite previous claims that they represent largely independent constructs.
Our work demonstrates the utility in using a multilevel modelling approach and the increased sensitivity of this analytic method.

In our data the ICCs (which assessed the extent to which scores or ratings were consistent within an individual) for internal details, vividness and (p)reliving were low (0.32 -0.55, see Supplementary Results).

This indicates that although the scores given by the experimenter for the episodic content and participants for their subjective experiences tended to be consistent, there was a lot of variability not due to individual differences i.e. due to situational factors, such as the cue words presented.

This aligns with the results and conclusions of Aytürk et al. (2024) who found that the amount of trait-like variance for vividness and reliving was 32% to 37% respectively, suggesting that at least 60% of the variance in memory ratings on certain phenomenological ratings is due to the specific memories.
text.formatted: This aligns with the results and conclusions of <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Aytürk et al. (2024)</ref> who found that the amount of trait-like variance for vividness and reliving was 32% to 37% respectively, suggesting that at least 60% of the variance in memory ratings on certain phenomenological ratings is due to the specific memories.

text.text: This supports the use of a statistical approach which can account for this variability.
This issue may help explain inconsistencies in the existing literature.
Many previous studies have relied on aggregated scores or examined only a single memory per participant, ignoring any cue-related variance.

Consistent with this interpretation, when we aggregated phenomenological ratings across narrative events (e.g. all vividness ratings for past memories) and correlated with aggregates of AI scores for the same events, most of these were not statistically significant.
The overall pattern generally echoed that observed in the multilevel analyses, but only the strongest relationships remained detectable using this less sensitive approach.
Thus, it is likely that the reason our results diverge from other studies, such as Clark and Maguire (2020) and Zaman et al. (2024) is due to our use of a more rigorous analysis method.
text.formatted: Thus, it is likely that the reason our results diverge from other studies, such as Clark and Maguire (2020) and <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Zaman et al. (2024)</ref> is due to our use of a more rigorous analysis method.

text.text: Although it should also be noted that Zaman et al. (2024) examined only one event per condition and collected written responses online, whereas our study used verbal narratives collected face-to-face.
text.formatted: Although it should also be noted that <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Zaman et al. (2024)</ref> examined only one event per condition and collected written responses online, whereas our study used verbal narratives collected face-to-face.

text.text: Given evidence that written and spoken autobiographical recall can differ in important ways (Bunnell et al., 2020; Pearson et al., 2023), methodological factors may also contribute to discrepancies across studies.
text.formatted: Given evidence that written and spoken autobiographical recall can differ in important ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Bunnell et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Pearson et al., 2023)</ref>, methodological factors may also contribute to discrepancies across studies.

text.text: Whilst the current evidence indicates a meaningful relationship between subjective autonoetic experience, as indexed by ratings of vividness and (p)reliving, and quantitative measures of episodic content, as defined by the AI protocol, the effect sizes are modest.

While Cohen's (1992) rule-of-thumb criteria can be used i.e. small (R² = .02), medium (R² = .13), or large (R² = .26), caution needs to be adopted given they are somewhat arbitrary and depend upon the research context (see Rights & Cole, 2018).
text.formatted: While <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Cohen's (1992)</ref> rule-of-thumb criteria can be used i.e. small (R² = .02), medium (R² = .13), or large (R² = .26), caution needs to be adopted given they are somewhat arbitrary and depend upon the research context (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Rights & Cole, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: There is currently no set of standardised effect size measures which have been widely adopted by researchers using multilevel models, so it is difficult to compare across studies e.g. no R² measures in the work by Devitt et al. (2017) or Aytürk et al. (2024).
text.formatted: There is currently no set of standardised effect size measures which have been widely adopted by researchers using multilevel models, so it is difficult to compare across studies e.g. no R² measures in the work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Devitt et al. (2017)</ref> or <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Aytürk et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: There are several a priori reasons to think that the magnitude of the relationship we would obtain might be moderate.
First, the way the AI is scored is according to the 'benefit of the doubt' rule, whereby any detail that could reasonably be considered internal is categorised in this way (Levine et al., 2002).
text.formatted: First, the way the AI is scored is according to the 'benefit of the doubt' rule, whereby any detail that could reasonably be considered internal is categorised in this way <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Levine et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The rule is designed to be lenient towards episodic memory, ensuring that rich, specific details (internal details) are not mistakenly disregarded as generic, repeated or semantic information (external details).
This avoids a false positive classification of a memory deficit based upon incidental factors yet might dilute associations between participant ratings and experimenter ones using the AI.
Second, there are cases where the two aspects of memory diverge.
One example is the neuropsychological case M.L., who suffered a traumatic brain injury.

He had a profoundly impaired phenomenological experience, as indexed by reduced Remember responses in the classic Remember/Know paradigm (Tulving, 1985 (Tulving, , 1989)), but only marginal reductions in internal details (Levine et al., 2009).
text.formatted: He had a profoundly impaired phenomenological experience, as indexed by reduced Remember responses in the classic Remember/Know paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">(Tulving, 1985</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">(Tulving, , 1989))</ref>, but only marginal reductions in internal details <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Levine et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Dissociations have also been reported in a syndrome called Severely Deficient Autobiographical Memory by Palombo and colleagues (2015).
text.formatted: Dissociations have also been reported in a syndrome called Severely Deficient Autobiographical Memory by <ref type="bibr">Palombo and colleagues (2015)</ref>.

text.text: Their three healthy, high functioning participants demonstrated reduced internal detail generation only for remote time periods, but their rating of vividness was significantly reduced for all events recalled.

Finally, Addis et al. (2010) investigated the recall of personal past and future events and found that experimenter scored internal details were lower in the older adult groups compared to the young participants.
text.formatted: Finally, <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Addis et al. (2010)</ref> investigated the recall of personal past and future events and found that experimenter scored internal details were lower in the older adult groups compared to the young participants.

text.text: However, there were no differences in self-report measures, except that older adults reported experiencing greater emotional intensity when imagining the future.
This suggests that although the number of episodic details recalled is an important indicator of vividness and (p)reliving judgements, other factors also contribute to subjective ratings.
In this regard, modest effect sizes are unsurprising and suggest that episodic detail meaningfully aligns with, but does not fully determine, subjective experiences of vividness and (p)reliving.

Among the AI subcategories, event details showed robust and consistent associations with vividness and (p)reliving, evident across both studies and for both remembering the past and imagining the future.

Event details constitute the largest component of the AI internal category and encompass the happenings, actions, people and objects, i.e. those elements central to narrative coherence (Conway et al., 2009 , Sekeres et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Event details constitute the largest component of the AI internal category and encompass the happenings, actions, people and objects, i.e. those elements central to narrative coherence <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Conway et al., 2009</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">, Sekeres et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: A key aspect of the event category is the temporal unfolding of the episode.

In the following example, "My dad told me there was a problem with my car, so I phoned the garage to make an appointment and took it in later that day", several event details -the 'happenings' are being relayed but these have a strong temporal structure.
It is possible that our findings with the event category might reflect the temporal sequentiality/causal structure of the event details.
Specific autobiographical memories have a temporal and causal ordering of events (Shapiro et al., 2006), which is usually evident when people communicate these to others.
text.formatted: Specific autobiographical memories have a temporal and causal ordering of events <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Shapiro et al., 2006)</ref>, which is usually evident when people communicate these to others.

text.text: Indeed, Nelson et al. (2021) found that linguistic measures of narrative temporal structure were positively associated with AI internal details, while Habermas and Diel (2013) reported that narrative structure was related to independently rated vividness.
text.formatted: Indeed, <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Nelson et al. (2021)</ref> found that linguistic measures of narrative temporal structure were positively associated with AI internal details, while <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Habermas and Diel (2013)</ref> reported that narrative structure was related to independently rated vividness.

text.text: They argued that reliving depends partly on experiencing events in a coherent temporal sequence.

Taken together with the present findings, this evidence suggests that event details may contribute to phenomenological experience because both rely on a common feature: the temporal unfolding of an episode.
The results therefore provide further support for the AI as an index of episodicity and highlight the importance of narrative structure in subjective remembering.
The emotion/thought subcategory also showed reliable associations with vividness and (p)reliving across both studies and temporal conditions.
This finding is consistent with a substantial literature demonstrating close links between emotional experience and memory phenomenology.

Emotional intensity has repeatedly been shown to predict ratings of vividness, reliving, and mental time travel more strongly than factors such as valence or memory age (Talarico et al., 2004; see also Habermas & Diel, 2013; Reisberg et al., 1988 and reviewed in Rubin, 2005; Kensinger et al., 2011; Kensinger & Fields, 2024; Phelps & Sharot, 2008).
text.formatted: Emotional intensity has repeatedly been shown to predict ratings of vividness, reliving, and mental time travel more strongly than factors such as valence or memory age <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Talarico et al., 2004</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Habermas & Diel, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Reisberg et al., 1988 and</ref> <ref type="bibr">reviewed in Rubin, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Kensinger et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Kensinger & Fields, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Phelps & Sharot, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the emotion/thought category extends beyond emotion alone.
It includes references to feelings, thoughts, beliefs, expectations, and other aspects of an individual's internal mental state.
Unlike perceptual or spatiotemporal details, these elements represent internally generated experiences rather than properties of the external environment.
In this respect, they resemble what Andrews-Hanna and Grilli (2021) describe as the distinction between the "mind's eye" and the "mind's mind."
Because these details are closely linked to self-representation, they may contribute particularly strongly to autonoetic experience.
Remembering is not merely the retrieval of isolated details.
Autobiographical narratives also serve functions related to meaning-making, identity, and self-continuity (Conway et al., 2019; Fivush, 2011; Habermas & Bluck, 2000).
text.formatted: Autobiographical narratives also serve functions related to meaning-making, identity, and self-continuity <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Conway et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Fivush, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Habermas & Bluck, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Recalling what one thought or felt during an experience may therefore strengthen the sense that an event happened to "me" and facilitate re-experiencing rather than as a detached reconstruction of external circumstances.
Consistent with this interpretation, Su et al. (2026) found that memories richer in internal mental states were also judged as more personally important.
text.formatted: Consistent with this interpretation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Su et al. (2026)</ref> found that memories richer in internal mental states were also judged as more personally important.

text.text: Thus, emotion/thought details may be particularly influential because they capture those aspects of experience most closely tied to the self.

Intriguingly, St Jacques and Levine (2007) found using the AI that freely recalled emotional memories (both positive and negative) contained both more event and emotion/thought details relative to neutral memories but did not differ on other episodic details e.g. perceptual.
text.formatted: Intriguingly, <ref type="bibr">St Jacques and Levine (2007)</ref> found using the AI that freely recalled emotional memories (both positive and negative) contained both more event and emotion/thought details relative to neutral memories but did not differ on other episodic details e.g. perceptual.

text.text: Emotional memories were also rated as more vivid than neutral ones.
These studies together with our own suggest it is the event and the emotion/thought subcategories that are driving the association with vividness and (p)reliving.

This supports the claim that it is the narrative/evaluative features, which reflect their central meaning to the self, which contribute more to autonoetic consciousness i.e. the sense of reliving and vividness.
For the most part, the precise perceptual or spatiotemporal details seem to be less important in predicting autonoetic consciousness (see Habermas & Diel, 2013).
text.formatted: For the most part, the precise perceptual or spatiotemporal details seem to be less important in predicting autonoetic consciousness (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Habermas & Diel, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Perceptual and/or spatiotemporal details might be more important in determining other subjective aspects of memory, such as confidence or veridicality.
Furthermore, it is also likely to depend upon the goal of the participant e.g. creating a 'vivid' narrative for a listener versus recalling the details of an event with high fidelity.

Thus, future research would need to determine whether manipulating these variables would affect the specific subcategories of the AI found to drive alignment between subjective experience and episodic content.

One exception to the lack of association between specific detail and ratings of autonoetic conscious was observed between the time subdimension of the AI and phenomenological characteristics in Study 2 but not in Study 1.
This was evident as an interaction with temporal condition, such that for vividness it was present in the future thinking condition but not past.
Time is important when considering episodic memory as it is included in the definition of it -events must occur at a specific time and place (Tulving, 1985).
text.formatted: Time is important when considering episodic memory as it is included in the definition of it -events must occur at a specific time and place <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">(Tulving, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: It is notable that we only observed this effect in the future thinking condition.
One possibility is that temporal information plays a particularly important role in rendering future scenarios plausible.
Imagined future events are inherently less fixed than memories, so specifying when an event will occur may help transform a vague possibility into a concrete representation.

Some support for this interpretation comes from a study by Ernst and D'Argembeau (2017) who found that organising personal events on a mental timeline, including estimated time of occurrence, contributed to the person's sense of 'realness' of future events.
text.formatted: Some support for this interpretation comes from a study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Ernst and D'Argembeau (2017)</ref> who found that organising personal events on a mental timeline, including estimated time of occurrence, contributed to the person's sense of 'realness' of future events.

text.text: Since future events are often connected to personal goals and plans (Ben Malek et al., 2018), temporal information may be especially relevant when constructing prospective simulations.
text.formatted: Since future events are often connected to personal goals and plans <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Ben Malek et al., 2018)</ref>, temporal information may be especially relevant when constructing prospective simulations.

text.text: Given that this effect emerged in only one study, however, this interpretation remains tentative.

Across both studies the subjective ratings and the episodic content scores from the AI, were higher when participants recalled events from the past compared to future imaginings, consistent with previous research (Addis et al., 2008; Berntsen & Bohn, 2010; De Brigard & Giovanello, 2012; Thakral et al., 2019; Williams et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Across both studies the subjective ratings and the episodic content scores from the AI, were higher when participants recalled events from the past compared to future imaginings, consistent with previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Addis et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Berntsen & Bohn, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">De Brigard & Giovanello, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Thakral et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Williams et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Despite these differences in overall level, the pattern of associations between quantitative episodic content and subjective ratings was remarkably similar across temporal conditions.

This is consistent with neuroimaging work demonstrating common neural substrates across these abilities (Thakral et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2020), similar deficits in psychopathology (Hallford et al., 2018) and that there is a relationship between how well people can recall the past and imagine specific future events (Williams et al., 1996).
text.formatted: This is consistent with neuroimaging work demonstrating common neural substrates across these abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Thakral et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Williams et al., 2020)</ref>, similar deficits in psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Hallford et al., 2018)</ref> and that there is a relationship between how well people can recall the past and imagine specific future events <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">(Williams et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: This provides support for the constructive episodic simulation hypothesis (Schacter & Addis, 2007) which suggests that the episodic memory system plays a fundamental role in creating episodic future imaginings by retrieving and flexibly combining elements of past episodes into a mental simulation of a novel scenario.
text.formatted: This provides support for the constructive episodic simulation hypothesis <ref type="bibr">(Schacter & Addis, 2007)</ref> which suggests that the episodic memory system plays a fundamental role in creating episodic future imaginings by retrieving and flexibly combining elements of past episodes into a mental simulation of a novel scenario.

text.text: It is also consistent with Tulving's (2005) notion of episodic memory being part of a more general faculty, that makes mental time travel to the past and future.
text.formatted: It is also consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Tulving's (2005)</ref> notion of episodic memory being part of a more general faculty, that makes mental time travel to the past and future.

text.text: Interestingly, we found that some associations between subjective ratings and episodic details were stronger when imagining versus remembering.
Future events differ from memories in the way in which they are derived.
Participants were explicitly told to generate a novel event which could plausibly happen to them in the future.

Therefore, perhaps it is unsurprising that there would be more alignment between a future scenario that the participant has just created and described, and the questions they answer about that event immediately afterwards.

However, when recalling a past event, there might have been additional factors that informed subjective judgments, such as how confident the participant is in the accuracy of the memory (Pezdek, 2003), how often it has been rehearsed (Ritchie et al., 2006; Skowronski & Walker, 2005), and the extent to which an event has been important or meaningful to a person's life story (Bluck & Habermas, 2001).
text.formatted: However, when recalling a past event, there might have been additional factors that informed subjective judgments, such as how confident the participant is in the accuracy of the memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Pezdek, 2003)</ref>, how often it has been rehearsed <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Ritchie et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Skowronski & Walker, 2005)</ref>, and the extent to which an event has been important or meaningful to a person's life story <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bluck & Habermas, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Some support for the idea that the subjective contributions to future imaginings are reduced compared to autobiographical memory comes from the study of Zaman et al. (2024) who found that the factor structure, when imaging the future, was simpler compared to remembering the past.
text.formatted: Some support for the idea that the subjective contributions to future imaginings are reduced compared to autobiographical memory comes from the study of <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Zaman et al. (2024)</ref> who found that the factor structure, when imaging the future, was simpler compared to remembering the past.

text.text: It is therefore plausible that the subjective ratings given in the autobiographical memory condition were influenced by a range of other factors besides the episodic content in the narrative, whereas these aspects might have exerted less of an influence in the future thinking condition.
Despite the association between emotion/thought content and phenomenology, we observed no effects of cue word valence.
A likely explanation is that the cue words were only mildly arousing and, where ratings were available, negative cues were generally less arousing than positive cues.
This is not what is typically found (Lang et al., 1997).
text.formatted: This is not what is typically found <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Lang et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Previous studies have shown that cue arousal predicts both the production of internal details and elevated phenomenological ratings (Kensinger et al., 2011; Kensinger & Corkin, 2003; Phelps & Sharot, 2008; Sheldon & Donahue, 2017; Simpson & Sheldon, 2020).
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown that cue arousal predicts both the production of internal details and elevated phenomenological ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Kensinger et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Kensinger & Corkin, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Phelps & Sharot, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Sheldon & Donahue, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Simpson & Sheldon, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, stronger manipulations of cue arousal may reveal effects not evident in the present work.
In both studies, autobiographical narratives were collected before phenomenological ratings, consistent with most autobiographical memory research (see Sotgiu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In both studies, autobiographical narratives were collected before phenomenological ratings, consistent with most autobiographical memory research (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Sotgiu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Although this raises the possibility that ratings of vividness and (p)reliving were influenced by the details generated during narration, this order was chosen to minimise metacognitive interference that could bias recall.
Importantly, Sotgiu et al. (2025) found no differences in subjective ratings, including vividness and reliving, between narrative-first and phenomenology-first groups.
text.formatted: Importantly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Sotgiu et al. (2025)</ref> found no differences in subjective ratings, including vividness and reliving, between narrative-first and phenomenology-first groups.

text.text: While narrative-first participants reported fewer details overall, the proportion of cognitive and sensory/perceptual details did not differ, and they reported a higher proportion of affective-process words.
The authors argue that administering narrative tasks first may provide a more accurate index of the influence of emotional experiences on memory.
While future research could counterbalance task order, current evidence suggests that testing order is unlikely to account for the present findings.

Similar to previous work (e.g. Rubin et al., 2003; Zaman et al., 2024) we chose not to provide precise definitions of the terms vividness and (p)reliving (which we described as "if you were actually there"), allowing us to examine how participants naturally rated these questions.
text.formatted: Similar to previous work (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Rubin et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Zaman et al., 2024)</ref> we chose not to provide precise definitions of the terms vividness and (p)reliving (which we described as "if you were actually there"), allowing us to examine how participants naturally rated these questions.

text.text: Consequently, we cannot determine precisely which aspects of experience participants considered when making their ratings.

Some theorists regard autonoetic consciousness as a direct, pre-reflective property of recollection rather than as a quality that requires explicit judgment or evaluation of detail (e.g. Klein, 2016; Tulving, 1985 Tulving, , 2005)).
text.formatted: Some theorists regard autonoetic consciousness as a direct, pre-reflective property of recollection rather than as a quality that requires explicit judgment or evaluation of detail (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Klein, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Tulving, 1985</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Tulving, , 2005))</ref>.

text.text: Vividness may reflect not just the clarity i.e. whether the memory is clear or vague and dim, but also an emotional/interoceptive dimension. Ford and Kensinger (2016) distinguished "external" vividness, corresponding to the reinstatement of perceptual and sensory details, from "internal" vividness, encompassing pre-experiential bodily or affective states.
text.formatted: Vividness may reflect not just the clarity i.e. whether the memory is clear or vague and dim, but also an emotional/interoceptive dimension. <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Ford and Kensinger (2016)</ref> distinguished "external" vividness, corresponding to the reinstatement of perceptual and sensory details, from "internal" vividness, encompassing pre-experiential bodily or affective states.

text.text: This suggests that participants may interpret vividness broadly, encompassing not only visual clarity but also sensory, emotional, and interoceptive dimensions (see also Tooming & Miyazono, 2021).
text.formatted: This suggests that participants may interpret vividness broadly, encompassing not only visual clarity but also sensory, emotional, and interoceptive dimensions (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Tooming & Miyazono, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together these findings suggest that participants' ratings of vividness and (p)reliving may be shaped by a multitude of factors, such as perceptual, affective and self-referential processes.
Further research is required to understand what participants understand by these concepts and how this understanding might differ between individuals.

In conclusion, using multi-level modelling we found that participants' subjective autonoetic experience of autobiographical memories or events involving themselves in the future are tied to the quantity of episodic details in the narration.

Episodic content related to event details, as well as one's thoughts and feelings at the time of the episode -those features of episodic content that capture the storyline or narrative structure and have a central meaning to the self -are most tightly coupled with an individual's sense of overall vividness and (p)reliving of freely recalled cued autobiographical events.
This connection seems to be stronger for future thinking than in autobiographical memory.
Our findings provide a strong counterpoint to studies which have claimed, based on suboptimal analyses, that quantitative measures of content and subjective ratings are distinct constructs.

Further research is now required to determine what other factors contribute to participants' subjective memory judgements and how this set of factors might change or be weighted differently according to whether people remember the past or imagine the future, the way in which memories are cued and expressed, as well as any moderating individual differences.

In the main paper we detail the relationships that were found when participants were asked to rate the vividness and sense of (p)reliving, which are widely agreed core features of autonoetic experience for past and future events (Cordonnier et al., 2018; Habermas & Diel, 2013; Rubin et al., 2003 Rubin et al., , 2019;; Zaman et al., 2024).

text.text: Participants were also asked to give ratings for the clarity of their memories/imaginings broadly aligned to the internal detail subcategories of the AI.

These were: event/perceptual ('Details including people, objects, and surroundings...), time ('The time in which this event takes place...'), place (The location where this event takes place...'), and emotions/thoughts ('My own thoughts and feelings when the event takes place...').
Participants rated each of these dimensions on a scale of 1-7 (1= not at all clear,7= extremely clear and distinct).
Below we report the mixed-effects models we ran using these subjective clarity ratings and the corresponding experimenter scored indices.
All of these indicate significant alignment between the ratings given by the participant and the experimenter scored subcategories from the AI.
